## The Tohunga Suppression Act 1907

The Tohunga Suppression Act 1907 was a piece of New Zealand legislation that made it an offence to practise as a tohunga — a traditional Māori healer or spiritual expert. It remains one of the more controversial laws of the colonial era, touching on health policy, Māori cultural identity, and the enduring tensions between Western and traditional knowledge systems.

## Background: Why Was It Passed?

By the early 20th century, the tradition of the tohunga had already been weakened by colonisation. European diseases had proved difficult for tohunga to treat, which undermined confidence in traditional healing, and the whare wānanga (schools of higher learning) that had trained tohunga began to close. [[1]](cite://1/1)

Into this vacuum stepped a new type of practitioner — described as 'second class tohunga' — who lacked proper education and authority, and who were seen to exploit the superstitions of a people caught between two cultures, travelling from pā to pā (village to village) claiming to cure all manner of illness. By the early 1900s, these figures were regarded as a threat by both Pākehā and Māori authorities. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Health officials and police also lodged complaints that tohunga were endangering rather than enhancing Māori health — for example, by bathing the sick in cold water and administering alcohol. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1)

## Who Drove the Legislation?

The Act grew out of concern over the practices of self-appointed tohunga, and was supported by a number of influential Māori figures. [[5]](cite://5/1)

- The Te Aute College Students' Association was particularly critical, believing tohunga could harm patients and hinder Māori progress. [[5]](cite://5/2)
- Prominent Māori doctors Māui Pōmare and Te Rangi Hīroa (Sir Peter Buck) spoke out against tohunga practices. Pōmare strongly supported the Act's introduction, driven by what he saw as preventable Māori deaths. [[5]](cite://5/3)[[4]](cite://4/2)
- The bill was presented to Parliament by Māori member of parliament James Carroll and was supported by all four Māori MPs. For Carroll, the Act reflected his impatience with what he considered regressive Māori attitudes. [[5]](cite://5/4)[[6]](cite://6/1)
- A health official named James Mason was also instrumental in the Act's passage, following his return to New Zealand in 1906. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## What Did the Act Say?

The Act's preamble stated that any person who gathered Māori around them by practising on their superstition or credulity, or who misled any Māori by professing to possess supernatural powers in the treatment of disease, foretelling of future events, or otherwise, was liable on conviction to a fine of up to £25 or imprisonment for up to six months. [[5]](cite://5/5)

## Rua Kēnana and Political Motivations

The Act has been seen by some as primarily directed at the Ngāi Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana, who had established an independent settlement at Maungapōhatu in the Urewera from 1907. Carroll regarded Rua as a charlatan who was drawing the Tūhoe people into isolation, and local police had been watching Rua since May 1906 on suspicion of acting as a tohunga. [[5]](cite://5/6)[[8]](cite://8/1)[[6]](cite://6/2)

Despite this, Rua was never actually charged under the Act. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Enforcement — and Its Limits

In practice, the Act was rarely used. Few prosecutions were brought and even fewer convictions secured. Its main practical effect was to drive tohunga underground rather than eliminate the practice altogether. [[5]](cite://5/7)[[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1)

The case of the tohunga Hikapuhi illustrates this well — she faced years of complaints and investigations, yet when Apirana Ngata urged in July 1909 that she be prosecuted under the Act, Carroll's response in May 1910 was simply 'No action'. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## Treaty of Waitangi Concerns

The Act has also been viewed as a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi), as it challenged traditional Māori wisdom — considered one of the taonga (treasures) that Māori were promised under the second article of the Treaty. [[5]](cite://5/8)

## Repeal and Legacy

The Tohunga Suppression Act was repealed in 1962. [[12]](cite://12/1)[[5]](cite://5/9) Twenty years later, health authorities began showing a willingness to accept traditional healing practices as complementary to Western medicine — even recognising tohunga and incorporating their work into the mainstream health system. [[12]](cite://12/2)

While the Act was not an outright assault on all aspects of traditional healing, it reinforced a broader cultural message that 'tohungaism' was undesirable — a message that sat uneasily alongside the promise of the Treaty and the enduring value Māori placed in their traditional knowledge. [[9]](cite://9/2)[[13]](cite://13/1)

1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of primary health care and the medical profession in New Zealand from 1867 to the early 21st century. It documents the transformation from family doctors, nurses, and midwives delivering care in the 1800s, through professionalization and self-regulation (Medical Practitioners' Act 1867, nursing registration 1901, midwifery registration 1911), to the modern primary health care system. Key developments include district nursing services, Plunket (1907), and the 1941 agreement maintaining fee-for-service payments with government subsidies. The document examines challenges of a two-tiered system with free hospital care but expensive GP visits, and traces reform efforts from the 1970s onwards, including midwife autonomy re-establishment (1990), alternative practitioners' emergence, and patient rights activism. Major reforms in the 1990s-2000s introduced contractual arrangements with GPs, independent practitioner associations (IPAs), and primary health organisations (PHOs) based on population-based funding with higher subsidies for disadvantaged populations. The 2015 zero-fee GP visits scheme for children under 13 represents the latest access initiative. The document also details Māori health care practices combining natural medicines and spiritual healing with European medicine.

European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

6.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
6.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

7.text:
[Page 12] Healers unite Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori, a national body of Māori healers, was set up in 1993. It aims to be an authoritative and unified voice for traditional Māori healing, and to uphold, promote, protect and sustain its practice. It is the only legally constituted body that speaks for a large number of healers.

[Page 3] Healing practices Illness was treated by karakia and rituals, and also by rongoā rākau (medicinal plants), physical massage, and the use of water for sprinkling or immersion. 11.document_title: Traditional Māori Religion, Spirituality, and Sacred Practices: Comprehensive Study of Atua, Tohunga, Karakia, and Tapu
11.document_summary:
This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of traditional Māori religion and spiritual practices. It begins with creation mythology detailing Te Kore (the void), Te Pō (the night), and Te Ao Mārama (the world of light), followed by the separation of Ranginui (sky father) and Papatūānuku (earth mother). The text explains major atua (gods) including Tāne (forests), Tangaroa (sea), Rongo (cultivated food), and Tūmatauenga (war), and discusses whether Io existed as a supreme being in pre-European Māori tradition.

The document extensively covers tohunga (priests and experts) who served as mediums for gods and spirits, acted as diviners (matakite), and served as healers and ritual guides. Key spiritual concepts explored include mana (power from gods and ancestors), tapu (sacred restrictions), noa (freedom from restrictions), mauri (life principle), hau (vital essence), and wairua (spirit).

A major focus is on karakia—formulas of words chanted to communicate with gods. The document describes various types of karakia used for love charms, healing, warfare, and childbirth. It details major life-cycle rituals including tūā (naming ceremony), tohi (child dedication), and pure (spiritual empowerment), along with ceremonies such as ngau paepae (warrior empowerment), rāhui (tapu placement), and whāngai hau (ceremonial food offerings). Sacred places (wāhi tapu), shrines (tūāhu), and ritual objects like godsticks are discussed in relation to ensuring fertility and protection, reflecting the Māori worldview where spiritual forces permeate all aspects of life.

12.text:
[Page 9] The impact of colonisation Colonisation by Europeans had a significant effect on traditional Māori healing. Tohunga had limited ability to combat the diseases brought by Europeans. Though Western medicine was also relatively ineffectual at the time, this failure still strongly affected Māori confidence in tohunga . Some Pākehā missionaries attributed the spread of disease to a lack of Christian faith. As their own healers appeared impotent, many Māori accepted this explanation and turned to Christianity. Over time, the whare wānanga (schools of higher learning) which had trained tohunga started to close. The tradition of the tohunga declined.

15.document_title: Fields of Plenty: The Revival of Herbal Medicine and Medicinal Herbs Industry in New Zealand
15.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores the resurgence of herbal medicine in New Zealand, examining its historical roots, contemporary revival, and industry development potential. The articles trace how traditional Māori medicine (rongoā) and European herbalism were marginalized through 20th-century legislation but have experienced renewed interest since the 1980s. Featured practitioners demonstrate practical applications of wild-crafting and garden-based healing traditions. New Zealand's excellent growing conditions support cultivation of high-value medicinal herbs such as arnica, mānuka, kumarahou, horopito, and St John's Wort, with successful local initiatives like Tairawhiti Pharmaceuticals and Forest Herbs Research. Key challenges include international certification requirements (GMP standards), regulatory frameworks, and intellectual property concerns regarding indigenous Māori plants following the Wai 262 claim. The collection emphasizes tensions between holistic plant-based healing and scientific validation, while addressing global threats to medicinal plant species and advocating for conservation efforts and "barefoot doctoring" using readily available garden herbs as primary healthcare. The government's recent agreement to regulate medical herbalism signals growing recognition of herbal medicine's role in sustainable healthcare.

19.document_title: Tūhoe: Self-Determination, Cultural Identity, and the Struggle for Te Urewera
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the Tūhoe iwi (tribe) of New Zealand and their 150-year struggle toward self-determination and cultural restoration. It traces Tūhoe's resistance against colonial dominance, land confiscation, and systematic violence—including the 1916 arrest of Rua Kēnana and Te Kooti's legendary resistance. The narrative examines historical trauma from military raids and the 1921 repeal of the 1896 Urewera District Native Reserve Act that had granted them autonomy. Central to the document is Tūhoetanga—the essence of Tūhoe identity—and how the iwi maintains cultural continuity through traditional practices, tikanga programs, and intergenerational knowledge transmission despite 85% living away from their ancestral homeland. The text details Tūhoe's commitment to land rights and rejection of Crown offers excluding land return, culminating in the 2012 settlement including financial redress, control of Te Urewera National Park, and a pathway to self-governance. Through personal narratives and historical analysis, the document illustrates how Tūhoe pursues mana motuhake (self-determination) by reclaiming cultural practices, developing a 40-year blueprint for independence, and redefining ownership through mana whenua principles. The work demonstrates Tūhoe's resilience in maintaining traditions, rebuilding identity through wānanga and cultural programs, and navigating ongoing injustices while seeking existential healing and autonomy.

Environmental challenges include cyclone recovery and conservation efforts, while economic realities involve low wages, tourism, remittances, and aid dependence. A critical comparison between Western Samoa and American Samoa reveals how modernization and American individualism have paradoxically improved mental health outcomes while challenging cultural preservation. The work explores the fundamental paradox of Samoan society: communal values and cultural pride coexisting with oppressive social controls, limited economic opportunities, and psychological stress.

33.document_title: Rua Kēnana Hepetipa: The Māori Spiritual Leader, Messiah, and Legacy of Maungapōhatu
33.document_summary: This document chronicles the life and spiritual leadership of Rua Kēnana Hepetipa, a pivotal Māori religious and political figure. Born to Ngāti Kahungunu and Tūhoe descent, Rua emerged as the claimed successor to Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki within two years of the latter's death in 1893. Following a supernatural revelation on Maungapōhatu mountain in 1905-1906, where he encountered the archangel Gabriel and was baptized as Hepetipa, Rua established the "City of God" at Maungapōhatu in 1907. His community, the Iharaira (Israelites), adopted Nazarite practices and constructed Hīona (Zion), a circular meeting house modeled after the Dome of the Rock. Through strategic marriages to twelve women, Rua linked the Tūhoe and Te Whakatōhea tribes. The community initially succeeded but declined due to harsh conditions and infrastructure challenges. A pivotal moment came with Rua's 1915 arrest for illicitly selling alcohol, politically motivated due to his pacifist stance during World War I. This led to the April 2, 1916 armed police expedition—the worst police-Māori clash of the century, with two Māori killed. Rua's subsequent Supreme Court trial, the longest in New Zealand's legal history until 1977, resulted in his conviction for resisting arrest and imprisonment. Released in 1918, Rua rebuilt Maungapōhatu and attempted to create an economically viable community, though it ultimately failed. Despite government surveillance and the Tohunga Suppression Act, Rua met Prime Minister Joseph Ward in 1908, advocating for equal laws for Māori and Pākehā. His legacy as a visionary leader for a dispossessed people endures in New Zealand's cultural imagination.

34.document_title: James Carroll: Bicultural Pioneer, Māori Political Leader, and Land Administrator in New Zealand
34.document_summary: James Carroll (Timi Kara, b. 1857) was a transformative bicultural figure in New Zealand history, born to an Irish father and Ngāti Kahungunu mother in Wairoa. Raised bilingually with Māori as his first language, Carroll pursued a pioneering career bridging European and Māori worlds. He served as interpreter to Parliament (1879-1883) before winning the Eastern Māori seat in 1887, later representing Waiapu (1893-1908) and Gisborne (1908-1919). As the first Māori to hold the Native Affairs portfolio (1899-1912), Carroll became pivotal in Māori land administration. Key achievements include securing the Urewera District Native Reserve Act 1896, establishing Māori Councils and Land Administration Acts (1900), and implementing the Native Land Act 1909. Carroll advocated for Māori economic empowerment and equality, opposing Crown pre-emption of land and supporting leasing arrangements. He championed land management committees and body corporate structures for Māori landowners while opposing separatist movements like Te Kotahitanga. Despite facing intense pressure from Pākehā opposition demanding land alienation, Carroll implemented land incorporations and enabled Māori farming development. Though unable to prevent significant Māori land loss, his diplomatic skills and unwavering commitment earned him respect from both Māori elders and the Pākehā establishment.

35.document_title: Tūtekohi Rangi: A Māori Faith Healer and the Tūtekohi Movement
35.document_summary: Tūtekohi Rangi (c. 1871-1956), also known as Wiremu Retimana Rangi or Richmond Rangi, was a Māori expert in lore and carving from Mangatuna on the East Coast. From the 1930s, he established a reputation as a faith healer and tohunga, leading the Tūtekohi movement—an unregistered Anglican offshoot featuring religious meetings that attracted 200-300 followers by 1949. The movement held meetings across five locations, drawing invalids with tuberculosis and other ailments seeking cures. Meetings lasted 4-8 weeks, disrupting employment, domestic life, and children's schooling, prompting concerns from health officials and police. 36.document_title: James Malcolm Mason: Pioneer of New Zealand's Public Health System
36.document_summary: James Malcolm Mason (1864-1924) was a Scottish-born physician who became New Zealand's first chief health officer. After studying medicine in Edinburgh and Glasgow, he practiced in Portsmouth and Blyth before emigrating to New Zealand in 1895. Mason established the Ōtaki cottage hospital and gained prominence through his bacteriological expertise and public health advocacy. In 1900, he was appointed chief health officer following the Public Health Act 1900, which established one of the world's first national departments of public health. His tenure focused on preventive health, vaccination, sanitation, tuberculosis control, and Māori health. He edited the New Zealand Medical Journal, established tuberculosis sanatoriums, and influenced the creation of Plunket nurses. Despite recurring ill health, Mason served with distinction until 1909, later practicing privately and serving in WWI. He died in 1924, remembered for his far-sighted contributions to New Zealand's public health development.

37.document_title: Māui Pōmare: Māori Leader, Health Reformer, and Political Pioneer
37.document_summary: Māui Wiremu Piti Naera Pōmare (1875/1876-1930) was a transformative Māori leader and New Zealand's first Māori health officer. Born in Taranaki to parents with connections to Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Mutunga, Pōmare was educated at Te Aute College and studied medicine in the United States, graduating MD from American Medical Missionary College in 1899. As Māori health officer from 1901, he pioneered health reform initiatives including sanitation improvements and village inspections. He organized the 1901 royal hui at Rotorua and supported the Tohunga Suppression Act. Elected to Parliament in 1911 representing the Western Māori seat, Pōmare served in various ministerial roles under William Massey's Reform Party. His major achievements include securing compulsory registration of Māori births and deaths (1913), negotiating the West Coast Settlement Reserves Amendment Act (1913) to address land confiscation grievances, and chairing Māori recruitment during WWI. As Cook Islands minister (1916-1928), he increased funding and improved services. As Health Minister (1923-1926), he launched a safe maternity campaign that dramatically reduced puerperal sepsis deaths through improved asepsis techniques and midwifery training. Collaborating with Ngata, Pōmare established a royal commission into land confiscations (1926), securing compensation for Taranaki and Waikato. He died of tuberculosis in 1930, leaving a legacy of bridging Māori and Pākehā worlds while advancing indigenous welfare.

39.document_title: Hikapuhi: A Māori Healer and Her Legacy
39.document_summary: Hikapuhi (Te Hikapuhi Poihipi) was a prominent Māori healer born between 1860-1871 in Rotorua to parents of Ngāti Te Rangiunuora descent. She rose to prominence around 1905, calling herself a nurse rather than a tohunga, and traveled throughout New Zealand administering Three Star brandy as medicine accompanied by healing words. Though credited with miracles including curing blindness, her credibility suffered after a prominent chief died following her treatment. Government officials, including health officer Māui Pōmare, attempted to suppress her activities due to concerns about alcohol distribution, particularly to children. However, many Māori patients testified to her compassion and effectiveness, as she provided free medical care to those unable to afford European doctors. Despite petitions supporting her work and her acquittal by the Rongokako Council, official disapproval and the irresponsible actions of some followers undermined her practice. Her activities gradually ceased after 1913, and she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi represented both a symbol of Māori spiritual healing and European establishment failure, providing essential healthcare to marginalized communities.

40.document_title: Bush, Alice Mary: Pioneer Paediatrician and Family Planning Advocate
40.document_summary: Alice Mary Bush (1914-1974) was a pioneering New Zealand paediatrician and family planning advocate. Born in Auckland, she earned her medical degree from the University of Otago in 1937 and became the first New Zealand woman to achieve fellowship in the Royal Australasian College of Physicians (1955) and the Royal College of Physicians of London (1970). Bush established a thriving private paediatric practice in Auckland and was instrumental in developing paediatric services in New Zealand, founding the Paediatric Society of New Zealand in 1947. She is best remembered for her advocacy work in family planning, serving as president of the New Zealand Family Planning Association and securing medical association approval for doctors to work in NZFPA clinics in 1961. Bush championed women's health and children's welfare, believing planned families supported social stability. She died in 1974 at age 59, leaving a legacy memorialized through the Alice Bush Family Planning Clinic and Memorial Prize.

42.document_title: Hēnare Tomoana: Māori Chief, Political Leader, and Legacy of Self-Determination
42.document_summary: Hēnare Tomoana (c. 1820s-1830s) was a prominent Māori chief from Heretaunga, Hawke's Bay, descended from high-ranking lineages including Ngāti Hāwea. After converting to Christianity in 1852, he became involved in land transactions and military campaigns against Te Kooti (1868-1869). Lack of government compensation deepened his financial crisis, resulting in the loss of his Heretaunga block share by 1869. Disillusioned with government treatment, Tomoana emerged as a leading figure in the Hawke's Bay Repudiation movement from 1873, founding and editing Te Wānanga newspaper to educate Māori about land issues and European business practices. Elected to Parliament for Eastern Māori in 1879, he advocated for Māori land law reform and successfully introduced a bill establishing local Māori committees to adjudicate land titles, leading to the 1883 Native Committees Act. As a House member and senior chief, Tomoana became a principal figure in Te Kotahitanga, the movement for an independent Māori parliament, serving as Speaker of the Great Council. His major achievement was presenting a draft Federated Māori Assembly Empowering Bill to the native minister in 1893, seeking delegated power over Māori affairs. Known for his moderate approach balancing advocacy with pragmatism, Tomoana earned appointment to the Legislative Council in 1898, a position he held until his death in 1904. His legacy reflects a lifelong commitment to Māori self-governance and land rights protection.

43.document_title: Patient Safety Advocates Oppose Government Plans to Drop Therapeutic Products Act
43.document_summary: Patient safety advocates and legal experts express alarm over the government's plan to repeal the Therapeutic Products Act (TPA), which was signed into law in July 2024 and scheduled to take effect in 2026. The TPA would have modernized regulation of medicines, natural health products, and medical devices—bringing them under a unified regulatory framework similar to drugs. Critics, including Carmel Berry from Mesh Downunder and legal expert Dr. Laura Hardcastle, warn that scrapping the act will leave New Zealanders vulnerable to harm from inadequately regulated medical devices. They cite historical failures including surgical mesh implants, faulty pacemakers, and metal-on-metal joints that caused significant injury and cost ACC over $32.5 million in claims. The current 1981 Medicines Act is outdated and provides minimal pre-market assessment or mandatory reporting of adverse events. However, the Medical Technology Association argues the TPA represents regulatory overreach, claiming most medical devices already have overseas approvals and that harmonizing with international regulators like the US FDA and Australia's TGA is sufficient. Legal experts counter that the US FDA's 510(k) fast-track process has been criticized for insufficient rigor, allowing some devices to be licensed despite original models being withdrawn for ineffectiveness or harm.

[Page 1] Traditional Chinese medicine finding a place in New Zealand ByLiu Chen Journalist, RNZ (RNZ Chinese), RNZ Asia 2026 05 22 08:07:27+12:00 https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.ht ml?videoId=6395186517112 Auckland acupuncturist Selwyn Wong Doo still remembers a time when he was helping at his father's clinic wearing a school uniform. His father, William, opened the first Chinese medicine clinic in Auckland in 1939, eventually serving as the founding president of Acupuncture New Zealand. Wong Doo, 71, said his father was blindfolded and led to a monastery in China to learn his skills before practising in New Zealand. "I remember him saying that he got scared once and gave up acupuncture because one of his clients said he was doing witchcraft and had the police come and knock on his door," he said. Selwyn Wong Doo, 71, is a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner. His father stopped offering acupuncture treatment for a while, carrying on with Chinese herbs, massages and diet, before picking it up again in the 1960s. Acupuncture gained some prominence in North America in the early 1970s after The New York Times published a first hand experience of acupuncture and moxibustion in China in July 1971. That was just before US President Richard Nixon visited China in February 1972. "My Dad in those days had about a six months' waiting list of people wanting to come and see him because he would have been one of the very few around at that time," Wong Doo said. Selwyn Wong Doo's late father, William Naturally, Wong Doo picked up the skills and carried on the family practice. In 1977, a bill was introduced to Parliament to restrict the practice of acupuncture to registered medical doctors, physiotherapists or dentists, he said. While such professions typically didn't know about acupuncture, professional practitioners would not be able to continue to offer such services if the bill went through. In a bid to retain their roles, a small group of acupuncturists gathered in Auckland and started the New Zealand Register of Acupuncturists that same year. The organisation is now known as Acupuncture New Zealand. "I think a lot of people understand acupuncture now," Wong Doo said. Renjie Xi, vice president of Acupuncture New Zealand Traditional Chinese medicine has deep roots in New Zealand, with evidence of the practice dating back to gold fields in the 19th century, said Renjie Xi, vice president of Acupuncture New Zealand. Much of its modern history had been associated with Acupuncture New Zealand, he said, adding that the establishment of regulatory body Chinese Medicine Council in 2021 was something of a landmark for the profession. "Today, Chinese medicine is a fully regulated health profession under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act, with more than 1300 registered practitioners nationwide," Xi said. All practitioners must be registered with the council, hold an annual practicing certificate and demonstrate ongoing competence, he said. Acupuncture, herbal medicine and tuina (Chinese massage) were the most representative therapeutic techniques, which were also the most widely practised services in New Zealand, Xi said. Cupping, moxibustion, gua sha (scraping therapy) were common complimentary treatments, he said. Gordon Zheng with some traditional Chinese herbs Gordon Zheng's Beijing Chinese Medicine Clinic on Dominion Road in Auckland is a practice that offers a bit of everything. Having studied at an institute now known as the Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, he started one of the first few Chinese medicine clinics in Auckland in 1992. "We were the third in Auckland, I think," Zheng said. "I'd estimate that there are probably more than 200 clinics in Auckland now." Although his patients were predominantly Chinese at the beginning, these days Zheng has a mixture of patients from all ethnic backgrounds, with some using his services for more than 20 years. A patient being treated with acupuncture at Gordon Zheng's clinic. "Many conditions can be regulated with acupuncture," Zheng said. "For example, facial paralysis and strokes can both be treated with acupuncture, and even conditions such as hypertension and diabetes can be managed with it. Traditional Chinese medicine was an empirical science, he said. "It relies on doctors accumulating experience through long term clinical practice over many years," he said. Traditional Chinese medicine carried an element of risk if not handled well, he said. For example, he said, needles could be inserted too deep, or the toxicity of certain herbs unconsidered. Caren Chen explains the structure of a human knee joint. Operating on Auckland's North Shore for five years, Caren Chen's Happipuncture Clinic has gradually built a loyal client base. Chen trained for seven years at the Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, working at a hospital before coming to New Zealand. Traditional Chinese medicine was specifically tailored to an individual, and two people experiencing a headache could be given different herbs and acupuncture treatment, Chen said. "I think traditional Chinese medicine is more of a holistic view that combines heaven, Earth and humanity," she said. Chen believed the best care could be provided to patients when combining traditional Chinese medicine with Western medicine. As such, her clinic offers physiotherapy and massage services. Moxibustion at Caren Chen's clinic "For example, when treating patients with pain or neuromuscular issues, in addition to considering meridians and acupuncture points from a traditional Chinese medicine perspective, we also think about muscle anatomy and exercise science from a Western medical perspective," Chen said. "We can keep preserve the good parts of [Chinese medicine] traditions the essence of them while also continuing to learn from Western culture." Recognition of Chinese medicine appeared to have grown in New Zealand over the past decade, but there was a long way to go, Chen said. "I think more people in New Zealand are gradually becoming exposed to and accepting traditional Chinese medicine and acupuncture, and many are increasingly placing their trust in these treatments, I believe that is a positive thing," she said. "From the perspective of practitioners, we also hope to continue improving ourselves overall whether that's our professional skills, cultural understanding or English proficiency. "I think that is the only way traditional Chinese medicine can develop more successfully in Western countries." Chinese Medicine Council chair Paddy McBride Chinese Medicine Council chair Paddy McBride said awareness of the benefits of Chinese medicine was growing not only in New Zealand but globally. "Chinese medicine has a history of many thousands of years and has strong emphasis on staying well rather than waiting to seek treatment only when something has gone wrong," she said. "The Chinese Medicine Council of New Zealand would like all New Zealanders to know that the profession is regulated and that Chinese medicine is a safe, valid choice to meet their health care needs." McBride would like to see traditional Chinese medicine incorporated into and offered within the public health system, as it is in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan. "Currently practitioners are working in private practice, and the cost of treatment is beyond many who would greatly benefit from the different aspects of Chinese medicine." Caren Chen treats a patient with a massage. Jacqui Lunday, Health New Zealand's national chief for allied health, said the organisation recognised that cultural beliefs, traditions and practices could influence an individual's health experience and treatment preferences. "Practitioners are expected to demonstrate cultural competence as part of their core professional practice, which includes acknowledging and respecting culturally specific approaches, while ensuring care is delivered safely and aligns with recognised standards and best practice," Lunday said. A Ministry of Health spokesperson said traditional Chinese medicine was regulated similarly to other allied health professions such as physiotherapists, podiatrists and chiropractors. "While some allied health professional services are offered in the public health system (such as occupational therapy and speech language therapy), this does not routinely include traditional Chinese medicine," the spokesperson said. "Some traditional Chinese treatments, like acupuncture, can be funded by ACC." RELATED

[Page 1] A group of midwives in Te Wai Pounamu are on a mission of reclamation, empowering wāhine and whānau by embedding te ao Māori into every part of their practice. Ōhua Midwives is a Māori led practice based in Ōtautahi founded by four wāhine who saw a deep need in their rohe for a midwifery service embedded in te ao Māori. In 2025, Ilah Marie (Ngāti Porou, Whakatōhea), Toni Wieser (Ngāti Toarangatira, Ngāpuhi), Kerianne Harmon Becks (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Porou), and Kenzie Nahona (Ngāti Porou, Te Āti Haunui a Pāpārangi) graduated from Ara Institute of Canterbury as part of a record breaking cohort: 10 Māori and two Pasifika midwives, the largest ever at the institute. Marie said during their studies, they saw a great need for a kaupapa Māori midwifery service. "On our placements, we realised there was no practice that was kaupapa Māori or te ao Māori driven," she said. "We all decided while we were there that when we come out we'll establish one, especially for whānau in the east [of the city] … we just wanted to plug the gaps in our communities." With Māori and Pasifika making up just 10 and 5 percent of all midwives respectively in Aotearoa, the group hope more wāhine from these communities pursue a career in midwifery. In te ao Māori, the Maramataka, the Māori lunar calendar, guides many aspects of life, including birth and fertility. Each moon phase holds meaning, influencing everything from planting kai to whānau planning, rest, and renewal. The name of their practice, Ōhua, was born from this mātauranga. While reading the pukapuka Wawata by Dr Hinemoa Elder, a page opened to the phase Ōhua, which was a tohu the group said. "Ōhua aligns with nurturing relationships and grounding oneself, making it significant for whānau to seek support and prepare spiritually and mentally. "By honouring this phase, we encourage whānau to stay present, value the collective journey, and appreciate the shared process of bringing new life into the world." The group explained that in its traditional context, Ōhua was linked to growth, nurturing and life force. "Making it favourable for planting and cultivating resources, deriving from 'Hua' which can be defined as fruit, be abundant, to bloom or blossom." Reclaiming traditional birthing practices Central to the kaupapa of Ōhua Midwives is the Māori health model Te Whare Tapa Whā. It recognises taha wairua, hinengaro, tinana and whānau grounded in whenua. Marie said they began every experience with māmā and whānau by acknowledging the tapu of te whare tangata. Te whare tangata, in te ao Māori, can be translated as 'house of humanity,' a women's womb or uterus. "We know that when we are even putting our hands on that space, we incorporate whānau, te ao, all of our natural resources, like muka," she said. Muka is a fibre made from harakeke (flax) and is used to tie the umbilical cord (pito) after birth. In te ao Māori, the placenta is known as whenua, which can also be translated to land in te reo. It holds massive significance and is a representation of the connection between the newborn pēpi and the land. Traditionally, the placenta would be buried in a location significant to the whānau, like their ancestral lands to not only honour and nourish Papatūānuku, the Earth Mother, but ground the pēpi to its whakapapa. The rōpū said they honour the whenua in their practice and help explain its significance to whānau, passing down mātauranga they may not have. "The placenta is whenua. It's significant. We hold it with our highest respect," Marie said. They encourage ipu whenua, a woven or crafted basket made from natural materials, which the placenta can be placed and buried in. "Talking to [whānau] about ways that we can follow tikanga in a modern time is important, because a lot of whānau are removed from their whenua," Marie said. "Even if whānau can't access their original whenua, planting in a pot is symbolic, connecting culture with practice." In replacement of plastic modernised tools, they use mātauranga Māori. "We cut the iho (umbilical cord) with pounamu cutters or kōhatu and use muka instead of plastic clamps. "We teach whānau to prepare it themselves, weave it, tie it... so they learn whakapapa and the reasons behind it." Centring whānau in every birth The midwives also stressed the importance of a whānau based care. "Whānau are from all different regions, iwi everywhere around Aotearoa, so it's important we are actually connecting with them and being led and guided by them and their tikanga as well, is really important," Wieser said. "In midwifery, usually there's just one set standard of care, but in te ao Māori, we really chime in on what the whānau needs are and how they were raised and what they were brought up doing. "Speaking with nannies, papas, wider whānau gives us a foundation to care for them in ways they recognise." They said their care model weaves professional practice with whānau connection. "Some of our whānau say they've never had friendship from previous midwives, so they're relieved to meet us and know we're real people. That connection matters," Harmon Becks said. The group also spoke about the importance of holding space for whānau during the birth, when appropriate, allowing them to lead. "We stand back, let papas or whānau members catch the pēpi. We're just the background, but we empower them to lead their own birth," Marie said. Honouring those who paved the way While Ōhua is new, the wāhine said they stand firmly within a longer lineage of Māori midwives who paved the way. Harmon Becks said they have been inspired by wānanga and rangahau (research) made available to them by wāhine like Kelly Tikao, who has done significant mahi in the midwifery space, upholding mātauranga Māori. "We're doing this loudly, but we aren't the first. If not for the Māori midwives who came before us… all four of us wouldn't be here," she said. The wānanga through Kelly Tikao, Ngā Maia and Te Ara ō Hine Tapu Ora enrichened their mātauranga (knowledge), they said. "During our degree, we went outside mainstream education. 99.9 percent of that learning is thanks to her mahi," Wieser said. Growing the kaupapa Looking ahead to the future of Ōhua, Harmon Becks said they are looking to expand their services across Aotearoa. "We're big dreamers, but we make it happen. "We're planning our own clinic, growing Ōhua beyond Ōtautahi. We can't wait to support Māori graduates building this mahi with us." They want to encourage more wāhine Māori to enter the midwifery space. "Every whānau needs their own midwife, so be one for your whānau," Wieser said. "Midwives are big ass hype girls. We celebrate the strength of māmā. We're here whispering, 'Girl, you got this, you're strong, you are all the things,'" Marie added. The group said education and guidance across the overall health system is vital, especially as Māori midwives remain underrepresented Waipounamu. "Even one more Māori midwife in hospital can make a in Te huge difference in how whānau experience their care." Related

[Page 1] How colonisation created the state care to prison pipeline 2024 07 23 19:07:31+12:00 By Dr Rawiri Waretini Karena* On 24 July, the Abuse in Care Royal Commission of Inquiry's final report will be made public by the government. Ahead of the report's public release, survivors share their hopes for the healing process ahead. First Person Abuse in care is a colonial story. When I walked into the prison yard for the first time as a teenager, having never been there before I already knew 80 percent of the men in there. We'd spent the last 11 years growing up together in state care. That's when I knew there was a pipeline to prison; a pipeline that has spent decades sweeping up and funnelling Māori children from state care to prison. We talk about fractured homes, fractured families, and fractured communities, but what is the whakapapa of how they became fractured? Look at it this way: if I sold you a car and I had cut the brakes, and you went off and drove it and you crashed, who is responsible? You for driving, or me for cutting the brakes? This acknowledges that whilst we are responsible for our actions, we are not responsible for the hidden mechanisms that operate within the environment we are born into, privileging one faction at the expense of the other. For me, it's clear the issue leads right back to legislative policies of successive governments. You can't separate abuse in state care from our history of colonisation and indigenous oppression. The stories of survivors of state care their stories are all part of the colonial story. Family violence, sexual violence and child abuse were not a traditional part of Māori culture prior to colonisation. This is captured in a proverb that states, "He Mareikura, he taonga tuku iho ki waenganui ko Ranginui rāua ko Papatūānuku. He tapu te wharetangata" our women are a sacred conduit between heaven and earth, because they hold the holy house of birthing. Māori families traditionally lived in communities where a child was loved and nurtured, so harming a child was tapu because when one harms a child, they also harm their whakapapa, leading to serious consequences, as whakapapa was also considered sacred. But when the British arrived, they brought with them the colonial tool of assimilation, targeting indigenous children because they were the better bet to be assimilated to Western views and Western ways of seeing things, by being coerced into upholding Western pedagogies. In Aotearoa, the British created Māori experiences of stolen generations through distributing assimilation policies via legislation, establishing the Native Department in 1861. In 1867, they implemented the Neglected and Criminal Children's Act, which Oranga Tamariki can whakapapa back to, as well as the Native Schools Act 1867, which established an education system designed to assimilate Māori into Pākehā society by requiring that only the English language can be written or spoken in schools. This was enforced through severe corporal punishment. As an analogy, if you take a stone and you drop it into a pond, it creates ripples. The Native Schools Act 1867 represents that stone. The first ripple made the Māori language illegal. The second ripple saw te reo Māori banned by the state. The third ripple saw legal justification for beating and abusing tama ariki for speaking their native language. The fourth ripple saw the status of tama ariki changed from taonga to the lower status as a commodity. This led to the fifth ripple, where tama ariki over generations began experiencing abuse, neglect, and death at the hands of their caregivers, who experienced harsh corporal punishment in schools as children, and then in turn applied the same form of discipline to their tama ariki, leading to the children ending up in state care. From 1950 to 1999, more than 200,000 children were subject to state care abuse, perpetuating a never nding systemic cycle of fractured homes, fractured families, and fractured communities without any intergenerational insights into the insidious systemic mechanisms that created the problem in the first place. When this report comes out, I really want to see the government be brave and explore this cause and effect. So far, the coalition has been really good at criticising crime rates, establishing boot camps and pointing the finger at gangs. But they've been really slow to identify contributing factors and the root causes that led to these outcomes. The royal commission has been operating since 2018. It's collected the lived experiences of thousands of survivors and hard evidence that support both survivors' stories and the recommendations made. They have all the information they need to make informed, evidence based decisions. We've been here before the Waitangi Tribunal and the remuneration process came about because there was finally, a recognition that the inalienable, inherited rights that Māori held previous to and recognised under Te Tiriti o Waitangi were breached over numerous generations, leading to intergenerational poverty, loss of cultural heritage, and a near extinction of te reo Māori, and that these breaches led to the privileging of pākehā at the expense of Māori. But this has been accompanied by a certain political intentionality that has enabled what I call "historical amnesia", to pervade the country, perpetuating ideas about Māori riding a gravy train, as opposed to acknowledging a history of invasion, war, genocide and the confiscation/ theft of trillions of dollars' worth of lands, resources, and assets. We can't let that happen again. We must unpack this narrative about state care and how it came about, and that is what the government is scared to do. I want to encourage them to be brave and open, so we never have to repeat it. But they do not know how. Yet Māori, do. Because we have done this before as well. In 1906, 95 percent of Māori could speak their native language. Eighty years later, only 5 percent could. We've gone from generations who lost their reo to future generations of fluent speakers. When I look at the damage done to Māori children in state care, assimilation sought to disconnect them from their native voice, and cultural heritage, controlling the way Māori children perceive themselves. Because a people alienated from their cultural heritage are like a tree without roots, blowing to and fro, for they are not grounded and anchored in their whakapapa, customs, and language, becoming vulnerable to the manipulations of those who do not have their best interests at heart. Part of the healing journey enables Māori children in state care to reconnect back to their cultural heritage, whilst our country as a catalyst for change, embraces working together as Te Tiriti partners honouring our history whilst simultaneously ensuring our futures, from a place of aroha, humility, and compassion to build the type of respectful race relations that would be the envy of the rest of the world. * Dr Rawiri Waretini Karena is from Ngāti Māhanga, Ngāti Māhuta, as well as Ngāti Kaahu, and Ngāti Hine. He spent more than a decade in state care before being convicted of murder and spending more than a decade in prison. Since his release, Waretini Karena has become an expert in intergenerational trauma and alternatives to violence. He graduated with a PhD Doctorate of Philosophy in Indigenous studies in 2014, and was a lecturer on the Masters and PhD Professional Doctorate Program at Te Whare Wānanga o Awanuiārangi. He is a national and internationally published editor and author lecturing at Wintec specialising in counselling social work and mental health. [Page 1] Taulasea, or traditional healers, play a significant role in Samoan society, new study finds ByChristina Persico 2025 06 27 10:14:53+12:00 A new study has found traditional healers, or Taulasea, have a key role in Samoan society. The study was published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online. Researchers interviewed 14 Taulasea three were from Aotearoa and the others from Samoa. They were aged between 44 and 94 years old and practiced a range of healing methods. The findings revealed four major themes: sacredness of the Taulasea knowledge and practice; Taulasea specialisation; Taulasea methods and approaches; and holistic views that impact health. Lead author Professor Riz Firestone from Massey University said Taulasea play a sacred, community centred role "rooted in spiritual duty rather than commerce". "Healers diagnose holistically, combining prayer, plant based medicines, massage and dietary advice, and they act as gatekeepers, referring severe cases to westernised medical care," she said. "Present day lifestyle habits that are modernised, reliant on processed foods and sedentary lifestyles contribute to surging diet related conditions like type 2 diabetes and malnutrition. Taulasea advocate a return to simple traditional diets." https://www.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/dateli nepacific/audio/2018966384/unlocking the healing powers of samoa s p lants The study said traditional healers are often the first port of call for Samoans in need of care. "The healing practices of Taulasea are deeply rooted in a spiritual context, where their work is above mere employment and is perceived by them as a sacred duty," it said. "This sense of duty shapes how they conduct their practices, emphasising the role of service over financial remuneration. "Although it is difficult to validate the spiritual dimension of the Taulasea's work, as people continue to use their services as either a first port of call or simultaneously whilst seeking Westernised medicine, the perpetual use of traditional healing reinforces the value of their positionality in society." Taulasea also recognised shifts in practices due to the changing environment and conditions that people present to them, the study said. "The blend of traditional, cultural, spiritual, and scientific may provide a robust framework for addressing health issues and enhancing overall quality of life. "In some societies, there have been collaborative approaches, where Taulasea have played complementary role with Westernised doctors, but this has been largely regulatory towards traditional healers. "Nonetheless, both practitioners can coexist, but a model of care and the nature of the collaboration requires further consultation between the two." The study also noted recent research that showed there may be "subjective benefits" that patients reap from seeing a traditional healer, that "may not be quantifiable in a Western framework", and so the subjective benefits must be further explored to get a deeper understanding of their work and role. "As global standards are shifting to incorporate more indigenous and traditional knowledge, it would be important to acknowledge the Taulasea still have a significant role in current modern day systems, and this could be capitalised upon. "What is currently needed is a further understanding of why people continue to use Taulasea; and how a reciprocal model of care be informed and developed for use in the future, where Samoans (and all Pacific people) have access to the best of both traditional and Westernised healing practices." The study also said the Taluasea were strict on patient commitment and compliance. "From the Taulasea's perspective, this is a critical part of their service, because should the patient not comply, the consequences are detrimental to the Taulasea themselves or their family members. "They believe that the sickness or illness transfers to them and/or to their family members; whether people regard this as being superstitious, it is a commonly held view by the Taulasea in this study from generational knowledge passed down to them." The study did note its limitations, including a small, non random sample size, possible translation issues, and its reliance on narrative interviews without other forms of methodological triangulation, such as a observational data. It details how Māori classified illnesses into mate atua (supernatural diseases caused by broken tapu and malevolent spirits) and mate tangata (physical ailments), with tohunga (priests) treating each through specialized methods including exorcism, purificatory rites, and herbal treatments. The document discusses how this act was repealed in 1962 and how rongoā experienced significant revival from the late 20th century due to resurgence of Māori culture, loss of confidence in Western medicine, and demand for spiritual dimensions in healing. Modern rongoā practitioners differ from traditional tohunga, with variable informal training and eclectic practices that often incorporate Western and other medical systems. The establishment of Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori in 1993 marks an important institutional development for Māori healers.

Colonisation by Europeans had a significant effect on traditional Māori healing. Tohunga had limited ability to combat the diseases brought by Europeans. Though Western medicine was also relatively ineffectual at the time, this failure still strongly affected Māori confidence in tohunga .

Some Pākehā missionaries attributed the spread of disease to a lack of Christian faith. As their own healers appeared impotent, many Māori accepted this explanation and turned to Christianity. 3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

4.fileDescription: Māui Wiremu Piti Naera Pōmare (1875/1876-1930) was a transformative Māori leader and New Zealand's first Māori health officer. Born in Taranaki to parents with connections to Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Mutunga, Pōmare was educated at Te Aute College and studied medicine in the United States, graduating MD from American Medical Missionary College in 1899. As Māori health officer from 1901, he pioneered health reform initiatives including sanitation improvements and village inspections. He organized the 1901 royal hui at Rotorua and supported the Tohunga Suppression Act. Elected to Parliament in 1911 representing the Western Māori seat, Pōmare served in various ministerial roles under William Massey's Reform Party. His major achievements include securing compulsory registration of Māori births and deaths (1913), negotiating the West Coast Settlement Reserves Amendment Act (1913) to address land confiscation grievances, and chairing Māori recruitment during WWI. As Cook Islands minister (1916-1928), he increased funding and improved services. As Health Minister (1923-1926), he launched a safe maternity campaign that dramatically reduced puerperal sepsis deaths through improved asepsis techniques and midwifery training. Collaborating with Ngata, Pōmare established a royal commission into land confiscations (1926), securing compensation for Taranaki and Waikato. He died of tuberculosis in 1930, leaving a legacy of bridging Māori and Pākehā worlds while advancing indigenous welfare.

He developed the technique of using a microscope to show people the micro-organisms that inhabited impure water. He also had slides of the various microbes to show to sceptics.

In a number of his reports Pōmare commented bitterly about the mortality that some of the new breed of tohunga caused; for example, by attempting to heal the sick by bathing them in cold water and administering alcohol. He strongly supported Carroll's introduction of the Tohunga Suppression Act in 1907.

Although Pōmare believed that the decline in Māori numbers could be halted by the correct medical methods, he also saw that the nature of the Māori population was changing; a new population with European ancestry was emerging and he considered that they would have the best characteristics of both races. Unlike Apirana Ngata , who was concerned over the loss of Māori identity, Pōmare welcomed intermarriage and Māori acculturation.

From 1902 to 1910 Pōmare reported to Parliament on his work in a series of exuberant reports in which he dealt not only with medical matters but also gave his opinion on a number of issues, including education and land tenure, at times earning rebukes from his superiors. These reports make it clear that he believed in the radical modernisation of Māori society even if this meant the loss of all Māori land. He considered that Māori should adopt a European lifestyle, become self-reliant and, above all, work.

6.fileDescription: James Carroll (Timi Kara, b. 1857) was a transformative bicultural figure in New Zealand history, born to an Irish father and Ngāti Kahungunu mother in Wairoa. Raised bilingually with Māori as his first language, Carroll pursued a pioneering career bridging European and Māori worlds. He served as interpreter to Parliament (1879-1883) before winning the Eastern Māori seat in 1887, later representing Waiapu (1893-1908) and Gisborne (1908-1919). As the first Māori to hold the Native Affairs portfolio (1899-1912), Carroll became pivotal in Māori land administration. Key achievements include securing the Urewera District Native Reserve Act 1896, establishing Māori Councils and Land Administration Acts (1900), and implementing the Native Land Act 1909. Carroll advocated for Māori economic empowerment and equality, opposing Crown pre-emption of land and supporting leasing arrangements. He championed land management committees and body corporate structures for Māori landowners while opposing separatist movements like Te Kotahitanga. Despite facing intense pressure from Pākehā opposition demanding land alienation, Carroll implemented land incorporations and enabled Māori farming development. Though unable to prevent significant Māori land loss, his diplomatic skills and unwavering commitment earned him respect from both Māori elders and the Pākehā establishment.

7.fileDescription: James Malcolm Mason (1864-1924) was a Scottish-born physician who became New Zealand's first chief health officer. After studying medicine in Edinburgh and Glasgow, he practiced in Portsmouth and Blyth before emigrating to New Zealand in 1895. Mason established the Ōtaki cottage hospital and gained prominence through his bacteriological expertise and public health advocacy. In 1900, he was appointed chief health officer following the Public Health Act 1900, which established one of the world's first national departments of public health. His tenure focused on preventive health, vaccination, sanitation, tuberculosis control, and Māori health. He edited the New Zealand Medical Journal, established tuberculosis sanatoriums, and influenced the creation of Plunket nurses. Despite recurring ill health, Mason served with distinction until 1909, later practicing privately and serving in WWI. He died in 1924, remembered for his far-sighted contributions to New Zealand's public health development.

8.fileDescription: This document chronicles the life and spiritual leadership of Rua Kēnana Hepetipa, a pivotal Māori religious and political figure. Born to Ngāti Kahungunu and Tūhoe descent, Rua emerged as the claimed successor to Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki within two years of the latter's death in 1893. Following a supernatural revelation on Maungapōhatu mountain in 1905-1906, where he encountered the archangel Gabriel and was baptized as Hepetipa, Rua established the "City of God" at Maungapōhatu in 1907. His community, the Iharaira (Israelites), adopted Nazarite practices and constructed Hīona (Zion), a circular meeting house modeled after the Dome of the Rock. Through strategic marriages to twelve women, Rua linked the Tūhoe and Te Whakatōhea tribes. The community initially succeeded but declined due to harsh conditions and infrastructure challenges. A pivotal moment came with Rua's 1915 arrest for illicitly selling alcohol, politically motivated due to his pacifist stance during World War I. This led to the April 2, 1916 armed police expedition—the worst police-Māori clash of the century, with two Māori killed. Rua's subsequent Supreme Court trial, the longest in New Zealand's legal history until 1977, resulted in his conviction for resisting arrest and imprisonment. Released in 1918, Rua rebuilt Maungapōhatu and attempted to create an economically viable community, though it ultimately failed. Despite government surveillance and the Tohunga Suppression Act, Rua met Prime Minister Joseph Ward in 1908, advocating for equal laws for Māori and Pākehā. His legacy as a visionary leader for a dispossessed people endures in New Zealand's cultural imagination.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

11.fileDescription: Hikapuhi (Te Hikapuhi Poihipi) was a prominent Māori healer born between 1860-1871 in Rotorua to parents of Ngāti Te Rangiunuora descent. She rose to prominence around 1905, calling herself a nurse rather than a tohunga, and traveled throughout New Zealand administering Three Star brandy as medicine accompanied by healing words. Though credited with miracles including curing blindness, her credibility suffered after a prominent chief died following her treatment. Government officials, including health officer Māui Pōmare, attempted to suppress her activities due to concerns about alcohol distribution, particularly to children. However, many Māori patients testified to her compassion and effectiveness, as she provided free medical care to those unable to afford European doctors. Despite petitions supporting her work and her acquittal by the Rongokako Council, official disapproval and the irresponsible actions of some followers undermined her practice. Her activities gradually ceased after 1913, and she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi represented both a symbol of Māori spiritual healing and European establishment failure, providing essential healthcare to marginalized communities.

13.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection explores the resurgence of herbal medicine in New Zealand, examining its historical roots, contemporary revival, and industry development potential. The articles trace how traditional Māori medicine (rongoā) and European herbalism were marginalized through 20th-century legislation but have experienced renewed interest since the 1980s. Featured practitioners demonstrate practical applications of wild-crafting and garden-based healing traditions. New Zealand's excellent growing conditions support cultivation of high-value medicinal herbs such as arnica, mānuka, kumarahou, horopito, and St John's Wort, with successful local initiatives like Tairawhiti Pharmaceuticals and Forest Herbs Research. Key challenges include international certification requirements (GMP standards), regulatory frameworks, and intellectual property concerns regarding indigenous Māori plants following the Wai 262 claim. The collection emphasizes tensions between holistic plant-based healing and scientific validation, while addressing global threats to medicinal plant species and advocating for conservation efforts and "barefoot doctoring" using readily available garden herbs as primary healthcare. The government's recent agreement to regulate medical herbalism signals growing recognition of herbal medicine's role in sustainable healthcare.

Under urgency, the first two readings passed with support of the three coalition parties on Tuesday. With debate ending for the night at 10pm, further debate and a vote on the third reading took place on Wednesday morning, passing 68 votes to 54. The Pae Ora (Disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill was introduced under urgency, prompting cries of outrage from the opposition. Health Minister Dr Shane Reti called it a "narrow bill" which "was canvassed at length on the campaign trail". "Substantively, this bill meets our hundred day commitment and delivers on our intent," he said at the outset of the bill's first reading. "While the particular version of the dream that the Māori Health Authority laid out is coming to an end today, I want to paint a different dream, one that will be outcomes driven, providing greater devolved decision making that will deliver care as close to the home and the hapū as possible. I say to Māori Health Authority staff to please join me, guide me, and help us together to row a different waka towards better health outcomes. This bill enables that."
